Other press reports also describe a national health identifier for each patient.
What is not settled

The bill is not law. Its final text, its dates and its fines may still change in Parliament. The 24-month period would only start once the technical rules are published, and those rules will say how a practice's software has to connect.

Until then, no one can honestly say that a program is compliant with Bill 52-26. What a practice can do is get its records into a shape that makes connecting easier when the rules arrive: digital, complete and well protected.
What already applies: Law 09-08 and the CNDP
While Bill 52-26 is still a bill, Law 09-08 on the protection of personal data dates from 2009 and applies today. It counts data relating to health as sensitive data.
Two of its articles matter most for a practice.
Article 57: processing health data without the express consent of the persons concerned can lead to 6 months to 2 years in prison and a fine of 50,000 to 300,000 DH, or one of the two.
Article 58: processing personal data without the security measures required by Articles 23 and 24 can lead to 3 months to 1 year in prison and a fine of 20,000 to 200,000 DH, or one of the two.

The CNDP, Morocco's national commission for the protection of personal data, oversees how the law is applied. It is the place to ask which declaration or authorisation your processing of patient data needs.

Data breaches do happen in Morocco. In April 2025, a cyberattack on the National Social Security Fund (CNSS) allegedly exposed information on nearly 2 million people, according to Moroccan media reports.
The wider picture
More patients now have health insurance. Generalising compulsory health insurance (AMO) covered more than 32 million beneficiaries in 2025, 88% of the population, up from 42% before generalisation.
More insured patients also means more claims paperwork for practices.
Public investment in digital is growing too. The Head of Government said it rose from 11 million DH in 2021 to more than 1.7 billion DH in 2024.
For dentists, the scale is clear. The 2025 health map (carte sanitaire) of the Ministry of Health and Social Protection counts 6,552 private dental practices, as reported by Aujourd'hui le Maroc.
If the bill passes as reported, each of them would have to keep a shared record up to date after every consultation.
What a practice can do now
List every place your patient data lives today: paper cards, spreadsheets, phones, an old program.
Ask for the patient's consent to process their health data, and keep a record of it.
Decide who in the practice may see which part of a patient's file, and make sure your tools respect it.
Protect what you already keep: computers locked when unattended, data encrypted, and backups that run on their own and are kept away from the computer.
Ask the CNDP which declaration or authorisation applies to your practice.
Move active patient records to software that encrypts data, controls access by role and keeps a log of who did what.
When the technical rules are published, ask your software vendor how and when they will connect to the shared record.
None of these steps depends on the final text of the bill. Each one is useful under Law 09-08 today.

Why practice software should keep working without internet · Sifra Labs
A practice runs on its calendar and its patient files. If either one depends on a connection or a server somewhere else, a cut line, an outage or an attack can stop the whole day.

When you choose practice software, it is easy to compare screens and prices. It is harder to ask what happens on a bad day: when the internet is down, when a computer breaks, or when someone tries to lock your data and ask for money. This article makes the case for software that keeps working on its own, and ends with a checklist to test your current setup.
When the connection drops

Software that lives on a remote server needs the internet to open a patient file or the day's calendar. Lines get cut, routers fail and providers have outages. When that happens, the patient is still in the chair.
Software that runs on the practice's own computers keeps working through all of that. The internet stays useful, but the day no longer depends on it.
Attacks that go after the backups too
Ransomware encrypts an organisation's data and demands a payment to release it. A backup is the way out, which is why attackers look for the backups as well.
In a 2024 survey by the security vendor Sophos, 67% of healthcare organisations said they had been hit by ransomware in the past year, up from 60% in its 2023 study.
Of those hit, 95% said the attackers tried to compromise their backups, and 66% of those attempts succeeded.
The healthcare sample was 402 IT and security leaders in 14 countries.
Smaller organisations are hit hardest. Verizon's 2025 report found ransomware in 88% of breaches at small and medium-sized businesses, against 39% at larger organisations.
Verizon also notes that smaller businesses are less likely to have up-to-date, readily available backups.
The trend is rising. In the United States, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) has reported a 264% increase in large ransomware breaches since 2018.
And when health data leaks, it is expensive. IBM's 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report puts the average healthcare breach at US$6.64 million, the highest of any industry for the 13th year in a row.
Morocco is not spared: in April 2025, a cyberattack on the National Social Security Fund (CNSS) allegedly exposed information on nearly 2 million people, according to Moroccan media reports.

The lesson is not that every practice will be attacked. It is that a backup on the same network as the computer it protects may not survive an attack, and that stolen data should be unreadable to whoever takes it.
Three design rules
Local first
The data lives on the practice's own computers, and every daily task works without internet: the calendar, the patient file, the invoice, the backup.
Encrypted at rest
The database is encrypted on disk, and the key is kept apart from the data. A stolen laptop or a copied file is useless without it.
Backups that happen by themselves

A backup that depends on someone remembering it will be forgotten on a busy week. Backups should run on their own, be encrypted, be able to leave the building on an external drive, and keep older copies for a while.
How we designed MeDoc Dentist
We applied these rules to MeDoc Dentist, the dental practice program we make and sell in Morocco. Here is what they look like in a real product.
MeDoc Dentist runs entirely on the practice's own computers. Appointments, charts, invoices and backups work without an internet connection, and patient data is not sent to a cloud.
The whole practice database is encrypted on disk with SQLCipher (AES-256). The key stays in the computer's secure keychain, not next to the data.
It backs up the practice once a day by itself, to a USB stick or an external drive if you choose one. Each backup is compressed, then encrypted with AES-256-GCM, and X-rays and scans are included.
It keeps the last 3 days of backups, one from last week and one from the last half-year, and deletes older ones automatically.
Every backup carries a cryptographic signature. A backup that was altered or damaged is flagged and cannot be restored.
Restoring takes one click. Before anything is replaced, MeDoc Dentist saves a copy of today's data, and puts it back if the restore fails.

In the Cabinet and Cabinet+ editions, the reception computer and the treatment-room computers share one database over the practice's local network, encrypted and with every change signed. A computer that loses the connection keeps working and catches up when it is back.

There are limits, and we say them plainly. The daily backup runs while the program is open, not in the background. And a backup drive only protects you from an attack if it is unplugged afterwards and kept somewhere else.

A checklist to test your own setup
Whatever software you use today, these checks tell you a lot.
On a quiet day, unplug the internet for an hour. Can you still open the calendar, a patient file and an invoice?
Ask where your patient data is stored: on your own computers, or on a server somewhere else. Who else can reach it?
Ask whether the data is encrypted on disk, and where the key is kept.
Find out when the last backup ran, and where it is. If nobody knows, assume there is none.
Keep one copy off the network: a drive that is unplugged after the backup and stored in another place.
Try a restore once, on a spare computer, before the day you need it.
Write down who to call when something goes wrong, and how quickly they answer.

How we look after your data and your code

When you work with us, you trust us with files, access and ideas. This page sets out the precautions we take as a company, from the first call to the end of the project. Our products have their own security pages.
What we do with what you share
These rules apply to every project and every conversation, from the first call on.
Only the access a task needs
We ask for the least access that does the job, such as a test account instead of an admin account. When the task is done, we ask you to remove it.
Ask for a non-disclosure agreement before you share details. We sign it before the conversation goes further.
Confidential by default
We use what you share only for your project. We never name you or show your work without your permission.
Your code is yours
Ownership of the code we write for you is transferred to you.
No patient records by e-mail
Please don't send patient records, customer files or passwords by e-mail. We never ask for them that way.
A secure transfer, agreed first
If a project needs real data, we agree with you first how it is shared, where it is stored and who can see it. Where we can, we work with test data instead.
Deleted when you wish
If you wish, we delete the data you gave us when the project ends, and confirm it in writing.
Support without your patients' data

When we help a practice that uses MeDoc, we don't ask for patient data. If we need to see a problem, we look at it with you on a screen you share. Support files stay on your computer until you choose to send them.
This website sets no cookies and runs no trackers or analytics. The contact form forwards your message to our mailbox and keeps no copy.
How we build
Security problems are easier to prevent than to repair. These habits are part of every change we make.
Every change is reviewed
We read each change before it ships and check what else it touches.
Tests run on every change
In our own products, every change runs the automated tests on Linux and Windows, end-to-end tests in a real browser, and a strict linter that fails on any warning.
Dependencies kept in check
We install exact, locked versions of every library. On every change, an automatic audit checks them against known vulnerabilities.
Nothing reaches you untested. Defects found in the 30 days after launch are fixed at no cost.
What we have not done yet
We are a young company, founded in 2026. We would rather tell you than have you find out.
No security certification yet.
We hold no security certificate, and no independent penetration test has been run on our products.
Our installers are not code-signed yet.
Windows and macOS may show a warning when you install our software.
